section.title: The Rise of False Teachers
section.sectionRationale: Having grounded the church in the sure word of God, Peter turns to the danger: false teachers will arise as false prophets once did. He exposes their methods and their doom, then proves from history that God both judges the ungodly and rescues the godly.
section.thesis: False teachers will secretly bring in destructive heresies and exploit the church for gain, but the God who judged the angels, the flood generation, and Sodom knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for the day of judgment.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the coming of false teachers, verses 1 to 3; God's pattern of judgment and rescue in three examples, verses 4 to 8; and the Lord's settled verdict, verse 9.

verses.text: Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be {{pseudodidaskaloi|false teachers}} among you. They will secretly introduce {{haireseis|destructive heresies}}, even denying the {{despotes|Master}} who bought them, bringing swift destruction on themselves.
Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed.
In their {{pleonexia|greed}}, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.
For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but {{tartaroo|cast them deep into hell}}, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment;
if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight;
if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the {{asebes|ungodly}};
and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless
(for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard);
if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to {{ruomai|rescue}} the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.

pseudodidaskaloi.gloss: A false teacher, one who teaches error while posing as a guide to truth. Peter warns that just as false prophets troubled Israel, false teachers will arise within the church. The danger comes not from outside but from teachers among God's own people.

haireseis.gloss: A faction, sect, or self-chosen opinion; here destructive heresies. The word behind heresy means a divisive teaching that splits from the truth. Peter says these will be introduced secretly, smuggled in, and they lead to ruin.

despotes.gloss: A master, sovereign owner, the word behind despot. The false teachers deny the Master who bought them, rejecting the very Lord who has a rightful claim over them. It underscores both Christ's ownership and the treachery of their denial.

pleonexia.gloss: Greed, covetousness, the craving to have more. It drives the false teachers, who exploit the church for money with deceptive words. Greed is a recurring mark of the false teacher, who serves his own gain rather than God's flock.

tartaroo.gloss: To cast into Tartarus, the deepest place of confinement. This rare verb pictures God consigning the sinning angels to chains of darkness to await judgment. It shows that even angelic rebels do not escape God's justice.

asebes.gloss: Ungodly, irreverent, without fear of God. Sodom's ashes stand as an example of what is coming on the ungodly. The word marks those whose lives are set against God and who share the doom Peter warns of.

ruomai.gloss: To rescue, deliver, draw out of danger. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, as He drew out Noah and Lot. The same God who judges the wicked is mighty and faithful to deliver His own.

basic.context: Peter now warns of the threat he has been building toward. Just as Israel had false prophets, the church will have false teachers who quietly bring in destructive lies, even denying the Lord who bought them, and who exploit people out of greed. Their judgment is certain. To prove God will deal with them, Peter gives three examples from history: the angels who sinned, the flood in Noah's day, and Sodom and Gomorrah. In each case God judged the wicked but rescued the righteous, Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to save the godly and punish the ungodly.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter closely parallels Jude, and both draw on the same stock examples of judgment. The key debate is the phrase the Master who bought them: does it mean Christ died for people who then perish, or that they merely claimed His ownership? The passage is also a strong statement that God's judgments in history are real and are patterns of the final judgment, while His rescues of Noah and Lot are patterns of His faithfulness to save.
basic.originalLanguages: The pseudodidaskaloi, false teachers, smuggle in haireseis, destructive heresies, denying the despotes, the Master who bought them, driven by pleonexia, greed. Peter proves God's justice: He used tartaroo, casting the sinning angels into the deepest confinement, drowned the ancient world, and made Sodom an example to the asebes, the ungodly. Yet He knows how to ruomai, to rescue, the godly, as He saved Noah and Lot.
basic.typology: The flood and the destruction of Sodom are types of the final judgment; Peter says Sodom's ashes are an example of what is coming on the ungodly. Noah and Lot, rescued from destruction, are types of God's deliverance of His people through judgment, foreshadowing the salvation secured in Christ. The judged angels warn that no rebel escapes.
basic.christ: The false teachers deny the Master who bought them, and that Master is Christ, whose blood purchased a people and whose lordship they reject. Christ is the Lord who both judges and rescues; the pattern of judgment and deliverance in these examples finds its center in Him, who saves His people through the judgment they deserved.
basic.god: God is shown as the righteous Judge who did not spare even angels, the flood generation, or Sodom, and equally as the faithful Deliverer who preserved Noah and rescued Lot. His judgment is certain and His rescue is sure. He is neither slow nor forgetful; the verdict against the wicked stands, and His power to save the godly is proven in history.
basic.crossReferences: Jude 1:4-8 gives closely parallel warnings and examples. Genesis 6 to 8 tells of the flood and Noah. Genesis 19 tells of Sodom and Lot's rescue. And Matthew 24:37-39 makes Noah's flood a picture of the coming of the Son of Man.
basic.oneStory: From the sinning angels to the flood to Sodom, the Bible shows a God who judges rebellion and rescues His own. Peter sets the coming false teachers in that long story: their doom is as sure as Sodom's ashes, and God's power to save the godly is as sure as Noah in the ark. The whole pattern points to Christ, in whom God finally judges sin and delivers His people.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with a contrast between 'then' and 'now' that reaches both ways, 'there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you', and the paragraph that follows is a single, enormous argument. Verses 4 to 9 are one sentence in the Greek: three 'if' clauses, each naming a judgment, followed by a single 'then' in verse 9. The sentence is built so that the reader has to wait for its verdict, and when it comes it has two halves that balance exactly, the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and how to hold the unrighteous for punishment.

The three examples are arranged so that rescue grows from nothing to something to someone. The angels, verse 4, are not spared and nobody is saved. The ancient world, verse 5, is not spared, but Noah is kept with seven others. Sodom and Gomorrah, verses 6 to 8, are condemned, and Lot is rescued, and Peter spends more words on Lot than on all the rest, three times calling him righteous in the space of two verses. The pattern opens up the point of the whole chapter: judgment is not random, and neither is deliverance.

The opening verses (1 to 3) turn on one repeated word. The heresies are heresies of destruction, they bring destruction on themselves, and in verse 3 their destruction 'does not sleep'. The false teachers deal in destruction and destruction is waiting for them. The verdict, Peter says, is 'longstanding', which answers the quiet unspoken thought that nothing has happened to such men so far.

There is a close parallel with Jude 4 to 13, where the same men and the same examples appear in a different order. The two letters share material, and the difference in arrangement shows that each author is working the examples to his own purpose. Peter has put the flood and Noah in the middle, so that chapter 3, with its flood and the flood of fire, has already been prepared.
context.historical:
Peter writes to churches that have already heard teachers who disagree with the apostles, as Paul warned the Ephesian elders, 'savage wolves will come in among you', Acts 20:29 and 30. In the Jewish world false prophecy was a well known crime, and Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 and 18:20 to 22 gave the tests for it: a prophet who led the people after other gods, or who spoke in the Lord's name what he had not been given. Peter's accusation that these men 'secretly introduce' error uses a word that suggests smuggling goods past a customs post, and in Galatians 2:4 Paul uses a related word of 'false brothers' who slipped into the church.

The examples in verses 4 to 8 were not Peter's invention. The Jewish writings of the period, among them Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, list the same judgments as standard warnings: the rebel angels and the giants, the flood, Sodom and the rescue of Lot. Peter is using a catalogue his readers would recognise, and every item in it comes from the books of Moses.

The picture of Sodom is sharper than the story in Genesis alone. Genesis 13:10 to 13 shows Lot choosing the well watered plain 'like the garden of the LORD', pitching his tent toward Sodom, and by Genesis 19:1 he is sitting in the gate, the place where a city's elders sat. Ezekiel 16:49 and 50 names the sins of Sodom as arrogance, overfed ease and refusal to help the poor, besides the abominations. Lot's distress in Peter's verse 8 is the moral cost of living there day after day, a daily wearing down.

The greed of verse 3 has a context too. Travelling teachers were a normal feature of the Greco-Roman world, philosophers and religious speakers who sold wisdom for fees, and the early church had its own rules for testing visiting prophets. Peter's charge is that these men 'do business' in the church with invented words, a fate Micah 3:11 had already pronounced on prophets who 'practice divination for money'.
context.canonical:
False prophecy is one of the longest threads in the Bible. Moses sets the tests in Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 and 18:20 to 22, Jeremiah says God never sent the prophets who 'ran with their message', Jeremiah 23:21, and Ezekiel is told to prophesy against those who prophesy 'out of their own imagination', Ezekiel 13:2. Jesus takes the thread up in the Sermon on the Mount, 'Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep's clothing', Matthew 7:15, and in the Olivet discourse, Matthew 24:11 and 24. Paul warns the Ephesian elders in Acts 20:29 and 30, and tells Timothy that the Spirit expressly says some will abandon the faith, 1 Timothy 4:1 to 3. Peter's chapter belongs to that unbroken line of warnings.

Each of the three judgments is taken up elsewhere. Jesus Himself pairs Noah and Lot in Luke 17:26 to 30, saying life went on in its ordinary rounds until the day the flood came and the day Lot left Sodom, and that it will be so 'on the day the Son of Man is revealed'. Hebrews 11:7 praises Noah's faith and says 'he condemned the world'. Ezekiel 14:14 names Noah beside Daniel and Job as men whose righteousness could deliver only themselves, a reminder that Peter's rescue of Noah and Lot is deliverance of persons, not of the cities they lived in. Jude 6 to 7 gives the angels and Sodom, and 1 Peter 3:19 and 20 speaks of the days of Noah and 'only eight souls' saved through water.

The picture of the Master who bought them looks both ways. Paul tells the Corinthians 'you were bought at a price', 1 Corinthians 6:20, and the heavenly song of Revelation 5:9 says the Lamb 'purchased for God' people from every nation. Deuteronomy 32:6 asks Israel whether the LORD is not the One who 'made' them, using a Hebrew verb that can also mean to acquire. Peter's language fits that language of ownership.

The book of Jude is the nearest relation, but chapter 2 also prepares chapter 3. Judgment by flood in verse 5 is the pattern for judgment by fire in 3:5 to 7, and the 'day of judgment' of verse 9 is the 'day of judgment and destruction' there.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter's purpose is to comfort and to arm. He wants believers who feel outnumbered by confident, successful teachers to know that those teachers are on a path with a known end. The three examples are not offered to frighten the faithful, they are offered to steady them, because every one of them is a case where the wicked prospered for a time and then did not, and where the righteous were afraid and then were kept.

He also wants the readers to understand the nature of the danger. These teachers do not announce their error. They bring it in quietly, side by side with truth, and their motive is gain, not conviction. The mark of these men, in Peter's mind, is that they exploit the flock, and that is how they can be recognised. Teachings can be argued over for a long time, but a man who sees the sheep as a source of income has already shown what he is.

The long sentence of verses 4 to 9 ends on a promise the readers can lean on: 'the Lord knows how to rescue.' Peter does not say the godly will be spared trials. The word he uses is 'out of' trials, and Lot's example shows that the rescue may come in the middle of horrors. The readers are to hold on and not to imitate the compromise that made Lot's tent so near Sodom.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what false teachers do and what God does to them, and it describes the judgments of the past as examples. It does not tell believers to carry out judgment on their own. Peter does not command the church to hunt heretics; the verdict belongs to the Lord, verse 9. The prescriptive material of the letter is in chapters 1 and 3, where believers are told to grow in knowledge and to be diligent; this chapter gives the reasons.

It also does not teach that everyone who teaches imperfectly is a false teacher. The marks Peter gives are specific: heresies that deny the Master, greed, deception, depravity, and a following that mocks the way of truth. Honest disagreement among those who confess the same Lord is a different thing.

The account of Lot is descriptive, not a pattern for living in a corrupt place. Genesis records his compromise plainly, and Peter does not excuse it. He tells us only that his soul was tormented and that the Lord rescued him. The application is to share Lot's distress, not his closeness to the city.

debates.question: What does 'the Master who bought them' mean in verse 1?

views.label: A claimed or covenant ownership, never effective redemption
views.case: In the Reformed reading, 'bought them' describes the false teachers' outward profession. They belonged to the redeemed community, called Christ Master and stood in the church, yet they were never truly saved. There is an Old Testament parallel in Deuteronomy 32:6, where the LORD is said to have acquired Israel as His own, though many in Israel perished. Peter writes from the point of view of what they claimed, not of what Christ effectively did for them.

views.label: Christ died for them and they perish anyway
views.case: Others read the words plainly. The verb is the ordinary Greek word for purchase, used of believers in 1 Corinthians 6:20. They hold that the death of Christ was for all, and that those who deny the Master and come to destruction show that the redeemed can reject Him. This reading takes the seriousness of apostasy to the limit.

views.label: A purchase offered to all, denied by these men
views.case: A middle view holds that Christ's death is the ground on which the gospel is offered to every person, so that the Master has a claim over all, and these teachers are guilty of repudiating the very claim the cross established. Peter's focus is on the denial, not on a theory of the atonement.

debates.bearing: Peter does not stop to explain, which suggests it did not trouble his readers. The weight of the verse is that the men are denying the One who owns them, and that is a reason for dread, not for speculation. Whichever view is held, the verse warns that outward belonging to the church is no shelter.

debates.question: Who are the angels who sinned, verse 4?

views.label: The angels who followed Satan in his fall
views.case: Peter says only that God 'did not spare the angels when they sinned.' On this reading the reference is to the original rebellion of angelic beings, with Satan at their head, a fall that Jesus alludes to in Luke 10:18 and John 8:44. The imprisonment of verse 4 is the fate of those who rebelled and are held for judgment.

views.label: The sons of God of Genesis 6:1 to 4
views.case: Jude 6 and 7 pairs the angels who left their proper dwelling with Sodom, 'in like manner', and 2 Peter 2:4 to 5 sets the angels beside the flood. Many take this as a reference to the sons of God who took the daughters of men in Genesis 6, a reading strongly present in Jewish writings of Peter's day, in which these beings were angels.

views.label: Human line of Seth in Genesis 6
views.case: Augustine and many later interpreters took the sons of God in Genesis 6 as descendants of Seth who married outside the godly line, and some apply this to explain Peter's angels, but most hold that Peter says 'angels' and means angels, not men.

debates.bearing: Peter names neither the sin nor the place, and his argument needs neither. The point is the same under every reading: spiritual beings of great rank were not exempt, so no rebel can hope to be.

debates.question: Are the unrighteous punished now or only held for judgment, verse 9?

views.label: Kept in custody until the final day
views.case: The phrase can be read as God holding them for the judgment still to come, as the angels are 'held for judgment' in verse 4. On this reading nothing is said about conscious suffering between death and the last day.

views.label: Under punishment already while awaiting the Day
views.case: The Greek uses a present participle that can mean 'being punished', so some take it that the wicked already experience punishment after death and are kept thus until the final verdict. This is the traditional Christian view of an intermediate state.

debates.bearing: Peter says the wicked are reserved, and the emphasis is that the verdict is certain and has not been forgotten. The text does not give enough to settle the details of the time between.

study.originalLanguages:
Peter's vocabulary in these verses gives the passage its force. In verse 1, 'secretly introduce' is a compound verb built from the idea of bringing in alongside, from the same family as the word Paul uses of the 'false brothers' who slipped into the church in Galatians 2:4. The heresy is a smuggled cargo, not an open argument, and it arrives next to truth. Peter says the heresies are 'of destruction', apoleia, and then says the teachers bring on themselves 'swift destruction', apoleia again, and in verse 3 their apoleia 'does not sleep'. The same word three times in three verses leaves no doubt about where the road ends. The verb in verse 3 is a word for nodding off, so destruction is pictured as a watchman that never drowses.

The verb translated 'exploit' in verse 3 comes from emporos, a merchant, and the word 'deceptive' is plastos, something moulded or fabricated, the root of our word plastic. The teachers trade in the church with words made up for the occasion, and they treat the flock as a market. Peter will say in verse 14 that their hearts are 'trained' in greed, the language of athletes, and here the same idea of trade underlies it.

In verse 3 the 'verdict', krima, is 'longstanding' and 'remains in force'; the Greek says it is not idle, a word for a worker who has stopped working. The judgment has not stopped working, however long it seems to have been quiet.

The repeated 'did not spare' of verses 4 and 5 uses a verb, pheidomai, that Paul uses of the Father in Romans 8:32, 'He who did not spare His own Son'. The same God who did not spare angels or a whole world did not spare His Son for the sake of the guilty, so the severity of the one is the price of the other. In verse 4, the 'cast them deep into hell' of the BSB is a single verb built from Tartarus, a word in the Greek world for the deep place of punishment below Hades. Peter uses the language his readers would know, while the content is the Bible's own: chains and darkness, and a holding for judgment.

Verse 6 says Sodom was 'reduced to ashes', and calls it an example. The word 'example', hypodeigma, is a pattern to be copied or heeded, as in John 13:15 and Hebrews 8:5, and here it is a negative pattern for 'what is coming'. The Greek speaks of what is about to happen, which carries the sense of certainty in the future.

In verses 7 and 8 Lot is called righteous three times, a word, dikaios. The verb that says he was 'distressed' is a form of wearing out, and 'tormented' is basanizo, from the word for testing metal and later for torture, used of the torment of a servant in Matthew 8:6. The word translated 'trials' in verse 9 is peirasmos, which covers both testing and temptation, so that the Lord rescues from both.

The verb for 'hold' in verse 9 is tereo, to keep or guard, the same verb as in verse 4 and 'reserved' in 3:7, tying the three chapters together. The participle with it, kolazomenous, is present tense, which is the root of the debate above.

typology.fulfillment: The flood is the great pattern of judgment on a world that would not turn. Genesis 6:5 to 8 shows human thoughts as altogether evil, and the one man who found favor is kept in the ark with seven others. Jesus uses it as the pattern for His own return, Matthew 24:37 to 39, and Peter in 3:5 to 7 reads the flood as a promise that a later judgment, by fire, will come in the same way. The escalation is from a judgment that spared the earth and promised never to repeat it by water, Genesis 9:11, to the final judgment that closes the age. The type falls short in that the flood left Noah's own sinful line intact, while the last day will remove sin itself.

typology.type: Noah as preacher of righteousness, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Genesis does not call Noah a preacher, though it tells of his obedience and his faith, Hebrews 11:7. Peter's phrase, and the later Jewish tradition that Noah warned his generation, fit a man who built an ark in public view while his world carried on. He becomes a pattern of the faithful witness in a hostile age who is vindicated by the event. The escalation is in Christ, the true herald of righteousness, who proclaimed the good news and bore the judgment He announced. Noah saved only his household; Christ saves a people from every nation, and unlike Noah He preaches in the power of the Spirit and by His own death.

typology.type: Sodom and Gomorrah as an example, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Fire and sulfur from heaven, Genesis 19:24, ended two cities, and the smoke Abraham saw rising was 'like smoke from a furnace', Genesis 19:28. Peter calls the event an example of what is coming. Jesus too takes Sodom as a measure when He says it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for the towns that saw His miracles and did not repent, Matthew 11:23 and 24. The escalation is that the people of Sodom had never heard the gospel, and those who reject the Son stand under greater light. The type falls short because Sodom's judgment was temporal and local, whereas the last judgment reaches every nation.

typology.type: Lot rescued from the fire, verses 7 and 8
typology.fulfillment: Lot is drawn out by the hand, Genesis 19:16, 'because of the LORD's compassion for them', and Genesis 19:29 says God 'remembered Abraham' and brought Lot out. The rescue is not earned by Lot, who hesitates and bargains, and it comes through another's intercession, Genesis 18:23 to 25. This is a pattern of grace in the midst of judgment. The escalation is that Christ is the intercessor who does not merely ask for the righteous to be spared but bears the fire for them, Romans 8:34. The type falls short because Lot is brought out of a city, while believers are brought out of death into life.

study.christ:
The Christ of this passage is first the Master, despotes, and the fact that He is so named shows how seriously the false teachers err. They are not merely mistaken about a doctrine; they deny a person who owns them. The same word is used in Jude 4, where the men deny 'our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ'. Peter has just opened his letter calling Jesus 'our God and Savior', 2 Peter 1:1, and the one who is Savior of the faithful is Master over the false.

The ownership language points to the cross. Peter's first letter says believers were not redeemed with silver or gold but 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:18 and 19, and Revelation 5:9 says the Lamb purchased people for God by His blood. Whatever the debate about the false teachers, the phrase 'bought them' sets the cross in the background of the whole paragraph, so that their denial is a denial of a price paid. Titus 2:14 says He gave Himself to redeem a people for His own possession.

The title kyrios in verse 9, 'the Lord knows how', most naturally names the same Jesus, as it does in 3:8 to 10, and so the deliverer and the assessor of the wicked are one person. Jesus Himself uses Noah and Lot to describe the day when He is revealed, Luke 17:26 to 30, and so the examples of verses 4 to 8 are not only precedent but preview: the One who will come on the last day is the One who has acted in every earlier judgment and deliverance.

There is also a pattern of Christ in the righteous who are kept. Noah and Lot are saved by something outside themselves, an ark and the hand of angels, and both are saved because of the Lord's mercy. They are a shadow of the greater rescue in which the people of God are carried through judgment in Christ, who Himself went through the flood of wrath at the cross. We should not press every detail. The ark is used elsewhere as a figure of salvation through water, 1 Peter 3:20 and 21, but Peter here does not draw that line, and the passage's main point is the certainty of judgment and the faithfulness of rescue, not a hidden allegory in every verse.
study.god:
This paragraph insists that God is just in a way that no one can bribe, outrun or outwait. He does not spare angels, and Peter's readers could hardly imagine any being higher than they. He does not spare an ancient world that had built a civilisation, and He does not spare cities that looked secure. The word that describes His judgment is final, but never arbitrary. Every example comes after a long patience: Genesis 6 shows God grieved before He acts, and Genesis 18 shows Him listening to Abraham's plea before He rains fire.

The passage shows God as a Judge who discriminates. Abraham asked, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?', Genesis 18:25, and this paragraph is the answer: the righteous are not swept away with the wicked. That is a deep comfort. The same God who judges the world has His eye on the single household in the ark and the single man in Sodom, and He knows each of them by name.

He is a God who knows. The statement 'the Lord knows how to rescue' is not about technique, it is about knowledge and ability. Nothing about the trials of the godly takes Him by surprise, and no darkness is too deep to bring someone out of. Paul draws the same conclusion: 'The Lord knows those who are His', 2 Timothy 2:19.

A tension is allowed to stand. God is patient and God is severe, and the passage does not choose between them. Peter will explain in chapter 3 that the delay is for repentance, and here he explains that the delay is not forgetfulness. A world that forgets judgment will be judged, and a world that hears the warning is being treated mercifully.

This shapes worship and life. A God who is only kind would not be worth trusting when evil prospers, and a God who is only severe would not be worth approaching. The God of 2 Peter 2 is the One who 'did not spare His own Son', Romans 8:32, in order to rescue the guilty, and so the fear that the passage inspires is the beginning of gratitude.

crossReferences.note: Jude describes men who crept in unnoticed, who deny the only Master and Lord, and who stand under the same examples of judgment. Reading the two letters together shows that Peter and Jude were facing the same threat, and that the pattern of denying the Master and indulging the flesh was recognisable.

The wickedness that brought the flood is told here: every inclination of the heart was evil all the time, and the LORD was grieved. The verse also ends with Noah finding favor, which is the other half of Peter's balance, so that the judgment and the rescue are in the same paragraph of Genesis as in 2 Peter.

The LORD tells Noah to go into the ark because he has been found righteous in this generation. Peter's description of Noah as a preacher of righteousness stands beside this word, and the family that entered with him gives the eight of verse 5.

The narrative of Sodom's destruction and Lot's rescue. Verse 16 shows the angels pulling Lot out by the hand 'because of the LORD's compassion', and verse 29 says God remembered Abraham. It supplies the facts behind Peter's 'rescued Lot' and shows that the rescue was entirely grace.

Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will sweep away the righteous with the wicked. Peter's verse 9 gives the answer, and the fact that Lot is saved is the proof that God does distinguish, even though the city's righteous were fewer than Abraham hoped.

Jesus compares the coming of the Son of Man to the days of Noah, when people went on eating and drinking until the flood swept them away. The Lord Himself treats the flood as a preview of His return, which makes Peter's use of it more than a historical illustration.

Jesus joins Noah and Lot in one comparison. Ordinary life went on until the very day of judgment, and the same will be true on the day the Son of Man is revealed. It is the nearest Gospel parallel to Peter's pairing of the two rescues.

Moses tells Israel not to listen to a prophet who leads them after other gods, even if his sign comes true, because God is testing their love. Peter's teachers belong to this line, and the test is the same: does the teaching hold fast to the Lord who redeemed His people?

Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. Peter's picture of men who exploit the flock for gain is a long exposition of this verse, and the test Jesus gives, fruit, matches Peter's list of greed and depravity.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that after his departure savage wolves will come and that men from their own number will distort the truth. Peter writes about his own departure with the same expectation, and both apostles teach that false teaching arises from within.

God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. Peter says God did not spare angels or the ancient world; Paul says God did not spare His Son. The same verb joins both statements, and the sparing of the guilty has a cost that fell on the Son.

Paul says believers were bought at a price. The same picture of purchase lies behind 'the Master who bought them', and shows that the language of ownership, in the church's vocabulary, points to the cross.

study.oneStory:
This paragraph answers a question the Bible has been asking since Genesis 3: does God deal with evil? The serpent's lie in the garden was that there would be no death, and the story of the world after the fall is one long test of that lie. Peter takes three moments from Genesis, the angels, the flood and Sodom, and reads them as proof that God does act, and that He has always done so with a double edge, judging the rebel and keeping the faithful.

Behind Noah stands the covenant promise of Genesis 3:15 that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent, and the survival of one family through the flood is part of how that line is kept alive. Behind Lot stands Abraham, whose intercession reached into the gates of Sodom, and Genesis 19:29 says that God saved Lot for Abraham's sake. The rescue of the righteous is therefore tied to the promises that run through Genesis toward Christ.

The passage also looks forward. False prophets recur through Israel's history, and each warning to the prophet or the people is a step toward the final unmasking at the end of the age. Jesus' words on the Mount of Olives and Paul's farewell to Ephesus show that the church would face the same enemy, and Revelation shows the end of that enemy and the false prophet in the lake of fire, Revelation 19:20, 20:10.

The flood and the fire of Sodom were partial judgments, and Peter calls Sodom an example of what is coming. The full judgment arrives in chapter 3 and in Revelation 20:11 to 15, but so does the full rescue: God brings His people out and sets them in a new heaven and a new earth where there is no more death or mourning, Revelation 21:1 to 5. The pattern of the three rescues, from the ark, from the plain and from the world's last fire, runs toward that new creation.

The lesson for the story as a whole is that the Judge of all the earth is also the Saviour, and that the God who destroyed a world in Noah's day is the same One who sent His Son to be the ark for those who trust Him. The paragraph is a warning for the false teacher, but for the believer who feels like Lot in his city it is a promise: the Lord knows how.

sermon.title: “False Teachers among You”, Part One
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in 2 Peter, this message on 2 Peter 2:1-10 handles the rise of false teachers, their secret heresies and greed, and God's proven pattern of judging the ungodly and rescuing the godly. A clear, orthodox treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: How does Peter say the false teachers will bring in their errors?

options.text: Secretly, smuggling in destructive heresies while denying the Master who bought them.
options.note: Verse 1: the danger is covert teaching from within, not open opposition from outside.

options.text: By openly announcing that they reject Christ from the start.
options.note: Their method is secret introduction, not open declaration.

options.text: Through divisive teachings that split the church from the truth.
options.note: True to the word for heresies, though the stress is on how secretly they enter.

options.text: By forcing the church to accept them at the point of a sword.
options.note: The threat is deception and infiltration, not coercion.

quiz.q: What drives the false teachers, according to verse 3?

options.text: Greed; they exploit the church for gain with deceptive words.
options.note: Verse 3 names pleonexia, greed, as their motive.

options.text: A sincere but mistaken love for the truth.
options.note: Peter exposes self-serving greed, not sincere zeal.

options.text: A desire to profit from those they deceive.
options.note: True, that is the outworking of the greed Peter names.

options.text: Simple ignorance of what they teach.
options.note: The problem is willful, greedy exploitation, not mere ignorance.

quiz.q: Why does Peter recount the angels, the flood, and Sodom?

options.text: To prove that God certainly judges the ungodly and rescues the godly.
options.note: Verses 4 to 9: history shows both God's judgment and His deliverance.

options.text: To show that God's judgments are only ancient history with no bearing now.
options.note: The opposite: they are patterns of the judgment still to come.

options.text: To give examples of God punishing sin in the past.
options.note: True, but he equally stresses God rescuing Noah and Lot.

options.text: To entertain his readers with dramatic stories.
options.note: These are sober precedents, not mere entertainment.

quiz.q: What is the conclusion Peter draws in verse 9?

options.text: The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for judgment.
options.note: Verse 9 states both truths: sure deliverance and sure judgment.

options.text: That God rescues everyone regardless of how they live.
options.note: The unrighteous are held for punishment; rescue is for the godly.

options.text: That God is able to deliver His people even out of the midst of trials.
options.note: True, though verse 9 pairs this with the certain judgment of the unrighteous.

options.text: That the day of judgment has been indefinitely canceled.
options.note: The unrighteous are kept precisely for the day of judgment.

quiz.q: How should we understand the phrase denying the Master who bought them?

options.text: Whether it means claimed ownership or purchase, denying the Master is grave treachery bringing swift destruction.
options.note: Orthodox readers differ on the atonement's extent; Peter's warning against apostasy is the clear point.

options.text: It settles beyond dispute that Christ died savingly for every single person.
options.note: The phrase is debated; Peter's aim is to warn, not to settle the extent of the atonement.

options.text: It shows the false teachers reject the very Lord who has a rightful claim over them.
options.note: True to the treachery in view, though the finer debate remains open.

options.text: It means the Master never had any claim on them at all.
options.note: The text stresses His rightful ownership, which makes the denial so serious.

questions: False teachers arise from within and enter secretly. How can you and your church grow more discerning about teaching that sounds appealing but drifts from the truth?
Greed drove the false teachers to exploit the flock. Where might the love of gain quietly distort how you handle money, influence, or ministry?
God rescued Noah and Lot out of the midst of judgment. How does His proven power to deliver the godly comfort you in your own trials?
Lot was tormented in his righteous soul by the sin around him. Have you grown numb to sin you live among, and what would it look like to feel it rightly again?
The Lord knows how to hold the unrighteous for the day of judgment. How does the certainty of final justice steady you when evil seems to prosper now?

translationNotes.note: The Master who bought them renders despotes, sovereign owner; the phrase is variously understood in the debate over the extent of the atonement, but denotes Christ's rightful lordship denied by the teachers.
Cast them deep into hell renders the rare verb tartaroo, literally cast into Tartarus; a footnote points to the imagery echoed in 1 Enoch, used to affirm certain judgment.
A footnote notes a textual variant on to destruction, and that the example may be read as a warning to future generations of the ungodly.
